title: Toolbox guide
text:
MATISSE stands for MATLAB Toolbox for vital rates surveillance. It brings together methods for studying cancer rates. Read the scientific background in Advances in statistical methods for cancer surveillance research: an age-period-cohort perspective.
MATISSE includes the analyses available in the Age-Period-Cohort Analysis Web Tool. It also provides comparative APC analysis, methods for smoothing Lexis diagrams, and semiparametric APC analysis (SAGE). A Lexis diagram displays rates by age and calendar period. Use Related methods and publications to learn more about each method.
MATISSE is free to use. Open it in MATLAB Online, or use a local copy of MATLAB if you have a license. Check the current MATLAB Online access terms when you sign in.

title: Toolbox guide
text:
Design
MATISSE uses an object-oriented design. An object stores data or a fitted model. A class defines a type of object. A method is a function that works with that type of object. Start with these four classes:

A rates object stores rates by age and calendar period.
An apc object stores an APC analysis fitted to a rates object.
A tbl object stores a table of values with row and column labels.
A matrix object stores values and their uncertainty. It carries that uncertainty through calculations, so you do not need to write separate code for each step.

The core classes shipped in the toolbox:







Class
Purpose




rates
Age-specific event rates over time (Lexis diagrams); descriptive plots and age-standardized rates (ASRs)


apc
The new age-period-cohort model


epiphany
Exploratory comparative age-period-cohort analysis


capricorn
Hypothesis-based comparative age-period-cohort analysis


joinpoint
Joinpoint regression


sift
Singular-value adaptive kernel filtration


sage
Semiparametric age-period-cohort analysis


panko
Kernel smoothing utilities feeding into sift


tbl / matrix
Lightweight labeled-data and error-propagating array containers underlying everything above

title: Case study 2 · Premature mortality across world regions
text:
The question
Premature death is death between ages 30 and 70, the age range of the Sustainable Development Goal 3.4 target. The project follows premature deaths from cardiovascular diseases and from cancer in 13 world areas, using deaths and population by age group and year from the WHO Mortality Database. How do these causes change by age, by calendar period and by birth cohort, and how do generations compare?
The two figures below illustrate the method with one country, Australia, from 1970 to 2024.

Figure 1 · Anatomy of the New APC model
Cardiovascular disease mortality at ages 30 to 69 in Australia, females (pink) and males (green).

(A) Observed death rates in the 5 x 5 Lexis cells modelled (5-year age groups 30 to 69, 5-year periods 1970 to 2024), log colour scale; dashed diagonals mark the first birth year of each social generation and the orange line marks age 50. (B) Fitted cohort pattern at age 50, with 95% confidence intervals; solid for cohorts observed in mid-life, dashed for projected cohorts. (C) Local drifts: the annual percent change of each age group, with the net drift dashed. (D) Fitted temporal trend at age 50 (solid), the trend from net drift alone (dashed), and period deviations below. Grey bands: G, Greatest; S, Silent; B, Baby Boomers; X, Generation X; M, Millennials.
What to notice

In panel B, how do rates at age 50 change from the oldest to the youngest observed cohorts? Does the fall have the same speed in all generations?
In panel C, at which ages is the annual fall steepest? How does each age compare with the net drift?
In panel D, how large are the period deviations around the net-drift trend?

You can reproduce a figure like this yourself in Module 2; the generation bands come from Module 4.

Prepare your data
Follow Module 1. In short:

Get counts and person-years by age and year from your registry or from SEER*Stat or CI5 Plus. The Resources page links slides that show how.
Build a rates object: csv2rates() for a file in the NCI web tool format, or rates_make() for a table with age, year, cases and py.

title: Module 6 · Capstone: your own analysis
text:
Make it reproducible
The Europe case study follows a set of habits that make their results easy to check and to reuse. Adopt the same habits in your project:

One README with the purpose, the data sources and the run order.
Numbered scripts that each do one step and write to their own folder.
Never edit raw data. Read it, and write derived data elsewhere.
A data dictionary in every output folder: a small CSV that lists each file and variable with a description, unit and provenance.
Record your software: a script that writes the R and package versions to a text file.
Rerun without surprises: relative paths, and set.seed() wherever random numbers are used.
Read numbers from outputs, not from memory, when you write a report.

Social generations
Birth cohorts are narrow. Generations are broader groups that people recognize, such as the Baby Boomers, and they often differ in lifestyle, exposures and access to screening. The fitted cohort pattern (FCP) from Module 2 tells you the rate at a reference age for every cohort. If you average it over the cohorts of each generation, you can compare generations at the same age, which a simple look at period trends cannot do.

The proxy parents of a generation are the cohorts born 20 to 29 years earlier, when their members would have been aged 20 to 29 at the birth of the generation. Comparing a generation with its proxy parents asks: are children at higher risk than their parents were at the same age?






NoteObserved generations only



A generation can be compared at age 50 only if its members have reached about that age in your data. The model can also carry younger cohorts to age 50, but that is a projection, and projection is not covered in this course. The labs keep the cohorts observed near the reference age and leave the other generations out.

Sometimes the question is not “how high are the rates?” but “what fraction of deaths (or cases) is due to a given cause?” rates_share() builds a rates object whose events are the cause and whose offsets are all-cause events. fcp_share() then fits the model and returns the fitted cohort share at a reference age.

s <- fcp_share(ex[[1]], ex[[2]], ref_age = 50)
sh <- s$share[estimator == "direct" & cohort %in% observed_cohorts(ex[[1]], 50)]   # observed cohorts only

A log-linear model of a proportion is adequate only when the share is well below 1. fcp_share() warns if a fitted share exceeds 0.95. When a cause makes up most of the events (for example, all cancers among all cancers), interpret results with care.

title: Module 4 · Social generations and birth cohort
text:
Self-check

Who are the “proxy parents” of Generation X (born 1965 to 1980)?

People born in 1900 to 1920.
Cohorts born 20 to 29 years earlier, from 1936 to 1960.
The Millennials.


Proxy parents are the cohorts born 20 to 29 years before the generation’s first and last birth years, approximating the age of parents at the child’s birth. social_generations() lists them.



Why use a random-effects model to pool rate ratios across populations?

It allows the true ratio to differ between populations instead of assuming one common ratio.
It is faster than fixed effects.
It removes the need for confidence intervals.


Populations differ in their exposures and health systems, so assuming a single true ratio is unrealistic. The random-effects model estimates the average ratio and the between-population variance (tau2).



A fitted cohort share of 0.04 at age 50 for the 1955 cohort means…

4% of 50-year-olds in that cohort have the disease.
The rate is 4 per 100,000.
4% of the events (cases or deaths) at age 50 in that cohort are due to the cause.


A share is a proportion of all-cause events, not a rate per person. In the example, it is melanoma cases per cancer case.

title: Module 2 · The New APC model
text:
Why APC is hard
Age, period and cohort are linked by one equation: cohort = period - age. If you know any two, you know the third. As a result, you cannot attribute the linear part of a trend uniquely to period or to cohort. A steady 2% yearly rise in rates could be a period effect (everyone’s risk changes together) or a cohort effect (each generation starts higher than the one before), and the data cannot tell them apart. This is the classic identification problem of APC analysis.
The New APC model (Rosenberg, Stat Methods Med Res) sidesteps it. Instead of reporting parameters that cannot be identified, it reports quantities that can, called estimable functions, and it keeps the unidentifiable linear trend in one clearly labeled number, the net drift:

the net drift is the overall annual percent change in rates. It cannot be assigned to period or to cohort alone, so it appears in both the cohort pattern and the temporal trend;
everything else is curvature: how age, period and cohort effects bend away from straight lines. Curvature is identifiable, and it is where period and cohort effects show up.

The model is a log-linear regression on the rates of a Lexis diagram. By default matisseR fits it by weighted least squares on log rates with the covariance scaled for overdispersion (method = "wls", as in MATISSE). A Poisson regression is available with method = "poisson".

title: Module 2 · The New APC model
text:
Self-check

What does the net drift of an APC model measure?

The effect of the most recent birth cohort.
The overall linear trend of rates, as annual percent change, which cannot be assigned to period or cohort alone.
The difference between the oldest and youngest age groups.


The net drift is the one number that keeps the unidentifiable linear trend. It appears in both the fitted cohort pattern and the fitted temporal trend. Everything else in the model is curvature.



Which estimable function shows how rates at a fixed age differ between successive generations?

Longitudinal age curve (LAC)
Fitted temporal trend (FTT)
Fitted cohort pattern (FCP)


FCP plots the rate at a reference age against birth cohort. FTT plots the same age against calendar period, and the age curves (LAC, CAC) plot rates against age.



Local drift at age 70 is 1.8 (percent per year). What does that mean?

Rates at age 70 rose by about 1.8% per year over the study period, from period and cohort effects together.
Rates at age 70 are 1.8% higher than at age 69.
About 1.8% of 70-year-olds have the disease.


Local drifts are annual percent changes in the rates of each age group over time. They combine period and cohort influences, just as the net drift does.

title: Module 0 · Welcome and setup
text:
Welcome
Rates of disease and death, such as cancer incidence or mortality, change with age, with calendar period, and with birth cohort, the group of people born in the same years. Age-period-cohort (APC) analysis separates these three time scales so that you can ask better questions. Is a rise in rates a change affecting everyone at once, or a pattern carried by younger generations? Are two populations following the same trend, or different ones?
matisseR is an R toolbox for disease surveillance, built for this kind of analysis. It is an R port of MATISSE, the MATLAB toolbox for vital rates surveillance written by Philip S. Rosenberg, and it adds tools for comparing social generations and cohort shares. You will learn it by using it on synthetic examples and on real research projects.






NoteHow the course works



Every module has the same rhythm: read a short explanation, run the code in R, then check what you learned with a short self-check. Code samples use the synthetic example data that ship with the package, so they run in seconds. The case studies then show the same ideas on real data.

FAQ



Do I need to know R already?+



Basic R helps: running code, reading a table, drawing a plot with ggplot2. Module 0 gets you set up, and every code sample runs as written. You do not need any APC background.





Do I have to pay for anything?+



No. R, RStudio and matisseR are free. The MATLAB toolbox in Module 5 needs MATLAB, but you can use MATLAB Online in your browser with a MathWorks account; check MathWorks’s current access terms.





Is the real data in the case studies available?+



The code samples use synthetic datasets that ship with the package, so you can run everything yourself. The case-study figures come from research in progress, and their data come from public sources such as the WHO Mortality Database and European cancer registries.





Is matisseR peer reviewed or published?+



The methods are published; see the method papers. The R package is version 0.1.0 and is being developed. It has an internal test suite, and its comparison with the MATLAB toolbox is in preparation.





How do I ask a question?+

title: Resources
text:
Glossary

Age-period-cohort (APC) analysis

Statistical analysis of rates that separates the effects of age, calendar period and birth cohort.

Birth cohort

People born in the same years. In a Lexis diagram, cohort = period - age.

CAPRICORN

Comparative APC analysis: fits several groups together and tests whether their rates are proportional by age, period or cohort.

Estimable function (EF)

A curve built from the model that does not depend on how the unidentifiable linear trend is assigned: LAC, CAC, FTT, FCP and local drifts.

Fitted cohort pattern (FCP)

The model’s rate at a reference age for each birth cohort.

Fitted temporal trend (FTT)

The model’s rate at a reference age for each calendar period.

Lexis diagram

A grid of age by calendar period, holding events and person-years in each cell.

Local drift (LD)

The annual percent change in the rate at each age.

Net drift

The overall annual percent change in rates; the linear trend that cannot be assigned to period or cohort alone.

Overdispersion

Variation in counts beyond what the Poisson distribution allows. Real counts usually show it; capricorn(overdispersion = TRUE) allows for it.

Person-years (offset)

The population time at risk in a cell; the denominator of a rate.

Proxy parents

The cohorts born 20 to 29 years before a generation’s first and last birth years.

Rates object

The matisseR representation of a Lexis diagram: matrices of events and person-years by age group and period.

Social generation

A broad group of birth cohorts, such as the Baby Boomers (1946 to 1964).

title: Module 1 · Lexis diagrams and rates objects
text:
The Lexis diagram
A Lexis diagram is a grid with calendar period on one axis and age on the other. Each cell holds two numbers for a surveilled population: the events (for example, new cases of a disease, or deaths) and the person-years at risk. Their ratio is the rate, usually quoted per 100,000 person-years.
Because everyone ages one year per calendar year, a person moves diagonally through the grid. All people in the same diagonal were born in the same years, so the diagonals are birth cohorts. For a cell with midpoints a (age) and p (period):
\[\text{cohort} = p - a\]
A person aged 50 in 2000 belongs to the 1950 cohort. Every cell therefore carries all three time scales at once, and that is why APC analysis needs a model: age, period and cohort cannot be separated by reading the table.
lexis_plot() shows the same rates twice: over age and period (left), and over age and birth cohort (right). Here it is for the first example dataset, with cells combined to 5 years of age by 5 years of period:

R <- matisse_example(1)
R55 <- rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5)
lexis_plot(R55)







Figure 1: Synthetic melanoma-like rates in women (example 1), 5 x 5 cells. Left: age by period. Right: the same cells by age and birth cohort.





Rates rise steeply with age, which dominates the picture. To see period and cohort effects you need a model that holds age fixed. That is the subject of Module 2.






NoteIn the case studies



The Europe study models 5-year age groups from 20 to 84 in 5-year periods (for example, 1973 to 2017 for England). It is a Lexis diagram of exactly this kind.

Prepare rates for modelling
The APC model needs square cells (age and period intervals of equal width) and no zero counts, because it works on log rates. Three functions prepare a rates object.

Combine cells with rates_chunk()
rates_chunk() sums blocks of ages and periods. If the periods do not divide evenly, the leftover periods are dropped from the start, so the most recent data are kept:

R55 <- rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5)
rates_uni(R55)[, .(ages, periods, cell, events)]





ages
periods
cell

35-84
1995-2019

The 29 single years from 1991 to 2019 became five 5-year periods, 1995-1999 to 2015-2019. The first four years (1991 to 1994) did not fill a block and were dropped. The total number of events fell accordingly.


Fill zero cells with rates_fill()
Small populations produce empty cells. Example 3 is a small population with many zeros:

Z <- matisse_example(3)
c(zero_cells_before = sum(Z$Events == 0),
  zero_cells_after  = sum(rates_fill(Z)$Events == 0),
  fill_value        = rates_fill(Z)$fill_value)

zero_cells_before  zero_cells_after        fill_value 
            178.0               0.0               0.5 


rates_fill() replaces zero or missing counts with a small positive value (at least 0.5) so that log rates exist. If you have many zeros, combining cells with rates_chunk() first is usually better than filling.


Interpolate ages with rates_i5()
Registries often publish 5-year age groups. rates_i5() interpolates to single years of age; "linear" keeps the group totals, "cubic" gives smoother values:

A5 <- rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5)       # 5-year ages, single years of period
I1 <- rates_i5(A5, "linear")
c(age_groups_before = nrow(A5$Events), single_years_after = nrow(I1$Events),
  total_events_equal = sum(I1$Events) == sum(A5$Events))

Self-check

A woman is aged 50 at the midpoint of the period 2000. Which birth cohort is she in?

2050
1950
1900


Cohort = period - age = 2000 - 50 = 1950. The diagonals of a Lexis diagram are birth cohorts.



Why must zero counts be filled before you fit the APC model?

Zeros make the Lexis diagram non-square.
The model needs person-years, not events.
The model works on log rates, and the log of zero does not exist.


The New APC model is fitted to log rates (by weighted least squares by default), so every cell needs a positive count. rates_fill() supplies a small positive value; combining cells with rates_chunk() first reduces the number of zeros.



You run rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5) on 29 single calendar years (1991 to 2019). What remains?

Five periods; the earliest four years (1991-1994) are dropped.
Six periods; the latest four years are dropped.
Five periods; the latest four years (2016-2019) are dropped.


29 = 5 x 5 + 4. Leftover years are dropped from the start, so the most recent periods are kept: 1995-1999 up to 2015-2019.

title: Module 3 · Comparing populations with CAPRICORN
text:
Why compare, and what “proportional” means
You rarely care about one Lexis diagram alone. You want to compare women and men, two countries, or incidence and mortality. You could fit a separate APC model to each and compare the curves by eye, but that wastes power and has no formal test.
CAPRICORN (comparative APC analysis; Rosenberg and colleagues, BMC Med Res Methodol 2023) fits all groups together and asks a precise question: how are their rates related? Take the ratio of the rates of a target group to a reference group in every cell of the Lexis diagram. Five situations are possible:









Model
The ratio of rates…
Groups differ in…
Rates are parallel along…




PH-A
is constant
their overall level only
the whole Lexis diagram


PH-L
depends on birth cohort only
their cohort pattern
cohorts (diagonals)


PH-T
depends on age only
their age pattern
time, within each age


PH-X
depends on calendar period only
their period trend
cross-sectional age curves


NPH
depends on age, period and cohort
everything
nothing



“PH” stands for proportional: the groups’ rates are proportional in some sense. NPH (non-proportional) is the unrestricted model, equivalent to separate APC fits. Each PH model is NPH with some blocks of coefficients forced equal across groups. A likelihood-ratio test compares each PH model with NPH. A small p-value means the constraint is too strict: that kind of proportionality does not hold. AICc ranks all five models by fit and parsimony.
Why bother? When a proportional model holds, you describe the comparison with one simple pattern, and your estimates are more precise because they borrow strength across groups. When none holds, that is itself a finding: the groups truly differ in several ways.

title: Module 3 · Comparing populations with CAPRICORN
text:
Compare estimable functions
cap_ef() returns the estimable functions of every group under any of the models, plus the ratio of each group to the reference. It has the same comp codes as apc_ef(). Here is the cohort pattern ratio of B to A under the unrestricted model (NPH) and under the model that holds (PH-X):

Rs <- lapply(matisse_example(c(2, 1)), function(R) rates_fill(rates_chunk(R, 5, 5)))
names(Rs) <- c("B", "A")
S <- capricorn(Rs)
r <- rbindlist(lapply(c("NPH", "PHX"), function(m) cap_ef(S, "fcp", model = m)[type == "ratio"]))
r <- r[x %in% observed_cohorts(Rs[[1]], unique(r$ref))]   # observed cohorts only; no projection
ggplot(r, aes(x, value, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NPH = "#0B2E4F", PHX = "#7A2E6E")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NPH = "#0B2E4F", PHX = "#7A2E6E")) +
  labs(x = "Birth cohort", y = "Rate ratio, B vs A (log scale)")







Figure 1: Ratio of fitted cohort patterns, population B vs A, under NPH and under PH-X (95% confidence bands, logarithmic axis), for the cohorts observed near the reference age. The PH-X band is much narrower.

title: Module 3 · Comparing populations with CAPRICORN
text:
Self-check

In CAPRICORN, what does the PH-A model assume?

The ratio of rates between groups is constant everywhere on the Lexis diagram.
The ratio depends on birth cohort only.
Each group has its own age, period and cohort effects.


PH-A (whole Lexis diagrams parallel) forces everything except the overall level to be equal. The second option describes PH-L and the third describes NPH.



The global test of PH-L against NPH gives p = 0.0002. What does that mean?

PH-L is the best model.
The groups have identical rates.
There is strong evidence that the ratio of rates is not a function of birth cohort alone.


The test compares the restricted model with NPH. A small p-value means the restriction does not fit, so proportionality along cohorts does not hold.



Why are the confidence bands of the ratio narrower under PH-X than under NPH when PH-X holds?

PH-X changes the data.
The restricted model has fewer free parameters and borrows strength across the groups.
PH-X ignores the age effect.


Forcing blocks of coefficients to be equal across groups reduces the number of parameters estimated, so each is estimated more precisely. This only helps if the constraint is true, which is why you test it first.

matisseR (version 0.1.0) ports the core of MATISSE: rates objects, the New APC model with five estimable functions, and CAPRICORN. It adds the generation and share tools you met in Module 4. Several other MATISSE methods exist only in the MATLAB toolbox, which Philip S. Rosenberg wrote and which remains the reference implementation.



Method
What it does
MATLAB
Read more




Smoothing Lexis diagrams
Denoises a matrix of rates with a panel of kernel filters, keeping an optimal balance of bias and variance
sift, panko
Smoothing methods for Lexis diagrams


SAGE (semiparametric APC)
Smooths the observed rates with SIFT, then fits the New APC model to the smoothed rates. Gives smoother estimable functions, which helps most when counts per cell are modest
sage
Cancer incidence trends in successive social generations, JAMA Netw Open 2024


EPIPHANY (exploratory comparative APC)
Given K groups, finds the best-fitting partition into proportional subsets and non-proportional singletons, so you can group estimable functions as equal, parallel or unequal
epiphany
Comparative APC analysis, BMC Med Res Methodol 2023


Joinpoint regression
Piecewise linear trends with the number and location of knots chosen from the data
joinpoint
Joinpoint method paper


Standard plots and summary curves
The four standard plots of rates (versus period, age or cohort) and marginal summary curves

title: Case study 1 · Cancer in successive generations in Europe
text:
The project
This project fits age-period-cohort models to cancer incidence and mortality in 21 European populations: 16 national cancer registries and 5 countries with regional registries. It replicates for Europe the study of Rosenberg and Filho (JAMA Netw Open 2024), who analysed cancer incidence in successive social generations in the United States.
The question: are younger generations (Generation X, Millennials) at higher risk of cancer than their parents’ generation was at the same age, and does the answer differ by cancer, sex and country?

Builds Lexis diagrams of cases and person-years by age and period for each population, cancer and sex (5 x 5 cells, ages 20 to 84)

title: Case study 1 · Cancer in successive generations in Europe
section: Figure 1 · Anatomy of the New APC model
text:
Figure 1 · Anatomy of the New APC model
Rectum (C19-C20), incidence in England, women (pink) and men (green).

(A) Observed rates in the 5 x 5 Lexis cells modelled (5-year age groups 20 to 84, 5-year periods 1973 to 2017), log colour scale; dashed diagonals mark the first birth year of each social generation and the orange line marks age 50. (B) Fitted cohort pattern at age 50 with 95% confidence intervals; solid for cohorts observed in mid-life, dashed for projected cohorts. (C) Local drift of each age group; dashed, net drift. (D) Fitted temporal trend at age 50 (solid), the trend from net drift alone (dashed), and period deviations below.
What to notice

In panel B, how do rates at age 50 change from older to younger cohorts, in women and in men?
In panel C, at which ages are local drifts highest? How do they compare with the net drift?
In panel D, how large are the period deviations around the net-drift trend?

You can reproduce a figure like this yourself in Module 2.

Figure 2 · Generations and their proxy parents

Social generations (dark bars; Rosenberg and Filho, JAMA Netw Open 2024) and their proxy parents (light bars), the cohorts born 20 to 29 years before the generation’s first and last birth years. Baby Boomers 1946-1964, proxy parents 1917-1944; Generation X 1965-1980, proxy parents 1936-1960; Millennials 1981-1996, proxy parents 1952-1976. Arrows run from the proxy parents to the generation. Grey bands and letters: G, Greatest; S, Silent; B, Baby Boomers; X, Generation X; M, Millennials.

section: Figure 3 · Children versus their proxy parents
text:
Figure 3 · Children versus their proxy parents

Ratio of the mean fitted rates at age 50 of each generation (Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials) to those of its proxy parents, for incidence and mortality in women and men, pooled across up to 21 populations by random-effects meta-analysis, with 95% confidence intervals (log scale). Ratios for the Millennials rely on cohorts projected to age 50, which this course does not cover.
What to notice

Pick one cancer. Is the incidence ratio above 1 (more disease than the parents’ generation had at the same age)?
Does mortality follow incidence? Why might mortality ratios differ, for example because of screening or treatment?
Compare women and men.

In R: each point is fcp_contrast() results from many fits combined with pool_rr() (Module 4).

title: MATLAB examples
text:
Data and Lexis diagrams
These examples use the built-in SEER datasets. Start with Example data, then continue in order.

Example data
MATISSE includes 16 example datasets from the US Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program. A Lexis diagram displays rates by age and calendar period. Start with example 16 to explore the workflow before using your own data. Run the code below to load the data and fill zero cells. Set DELTA to 2 or 5 to combine age and period intervals when the data are sparse.
Example = 16;      % 1x1 age-by-period Lexis diagram, e.g. "F melanoma NHW"
DELTA   = 1;        % chunk to 2x2 or 5x5 age/period blocks if the data are sparse

r = ratesdata(Example);
switch DELTA
    case 1
        R0 = r;
    case 2
        R0 = chunk(r, 'AgeBlock', 2, 'PerBlock', 2);
    case 5
        R0 = chunk(r, 'AgeBlock', 5, 'PerBlock', 5);
end

R = fill(R0);   % add a small value to any zero cells
disp(R)


Visualizing a Lexis diagram
MATLAB toolbox video: Watch Visualizing a Lexis diagram on YouTube (43 sec).
Two plots help you explore the same data. A heat map uses color to show the rates; a 3-D surface shows log rates. Run the Example data section first to create R. Then run this code: pcolor(R) draws the heat map, and surf(R) draws the surface.
figure('Position', [0 0 700 700])
pcolor(R)

figure('Position', [0 0 700 700])
surf(R)



melanoma F NHW, 1992–2020 SEER rates per 100,000 — pcolor heat map


Graphics settings can make patterns easier to see. Run the code below to compare the surface on the left with a heat map on the right. The heat map uses the nepal color scheme. Change one option at a time and inspect the result.
subplot(1, 2, 1)
surf(R)
colormap nepal
colorbar off
shading faceted

subplot(1, 2, 2)
pvp1 = ego('class', 'rates', 'method', 'pcolor');
pvp1.colormap  = 'nepal';
pvp1.colorbar  = 'southoutside';
pcolor(R, pvp1)



Log-rate surface vs. heat map, same Lexis diagram


A property-value pair names a graphics setting and gives its value. The go options store these settings. Use ego to copy a plot method’s default settings, then edit the copy. MATISSE includes a 54-color line palette called clarinet. It also includes the africa and nepal color schemes, alongside MATLAB’s built-in choices.


Comparing several Lexis diagrams at once
Placing diagrams side by side helps you compare patterns across groups. Use thumbnail or vistagram with objects of the same size. Run the example below to compare breast cancer rates by estrogen receptor (ER) status and race. ER+ means receptor-positive; ER− means receptor-negative. NHB and NHW mean non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White. The code combines the data into 2-by-2 age and period blocks, then displays log rates.
r4 = ratesdata([1 3 2 4]);   % ER+ NHB, ER+ NHW, ER- NHB, ER- NHW
t4 = cell(1, 4);
for i = 1:4
    r4{i} = chunk(r4{i}, 'AgeBlock', 2, 'PerBlock', 2);
    t4{i} = type(r4{i}, 'comp', 'lr');   % log rates
end

figure('Position', [0 0 1200 600])
thumbnail(t4)



Thumbnail comparison of four Lexis diagrams: breast cancer log rates by ER status and race

Estimable functions
Fit the new APC model to a rates object with apc. The model provides estimable functions (EFs). These are summaries of age, period, and cohort effects that the data can determine. Run plot(M) on the fitted model M to draw six of them in one 2-by-3 panel:

'ld'

'cac'

Use ef(M, 'Comp', 'lac') to return one estimable function as a matrix object, which holds the values and their uncertainty. MATISSE provides all the outputs of the NCI web tool and more. The new age-period-cohort model defines each function. For options, run help apc/ef and help apc/plot.

title: MATLAB examples
text:
Advanced methods
These methods build on the new APC model. Each has a short description and a method paper. Live scripts will be added as they become available.

Smoothing with SIFT
Rates are noisy when case counts are small. SIFT (singular-value adaptive kernel filtration) smooths a matrix of rates with a panel of kernel operators. It combines their results into denoised values with an optimal balance of bias and variance. Read Smoothing methods for Lexis diagrams to learn the method.
Live script: coming soon.


Semiparametric APC with SAGE
SAGE (semiparametric age-period-cohort analysis) works in two steps. First, it smooths the observed rates with SIFT. Then it fits the new APC model to the smoothed rates. SAGE estimable functions are smoother than those from the standard model, which helps most when cell counts are modest. Run sage(R) to start. Read Semiparametric age-period-cohort analysis to learn the method.
Live script: coming soon.


Comparative APC analysis
Comparative APC analysis compares rates from several groups, such as strata defined by sex, race, or ER status, over the same Lexis diagram. The built-in breast cancer examples are a good place to try it.

EPIPHANY explores the data. It finds the best-fitting way to split the groups into subsets with proportional rates and single groups that are not proportional. You can then group estimable functions as equal, parallel, or unequal.
CAPRICORN tests hypotheses. It determines whether the rates are jointly proportional by age, period, or cohort. Proportional rates are easier to interpret and give more efficient estimates. A lack of proportionality shows that the groups differ significantly.

Read Comparative age-period-cohort analysis to learn the methods. For options, run help epiphany/epiphany and help capricorn/capricorn.

title: MATLAB toolbox
text:
MATISSE (MATLAB Toolbox for vItal rateS SurveillancE) was written by Philip S. Rosenberg. It implements the methods described in Filho & Rosenberg, Front Oncol 2024, and the R package matisseR is a port of its core. The MATLAB toolbox remains the reference implementation and still has several methods that R does not: smoothing (SIFT), SAGE, EPIPHANY, joinpoint regression and the standard plots. Module 5 explains when to use it.
MATISSE is free to use through MATLAB Online with a MathWorks account (check MathWorks’s current access terms), or locally if you have a MATLAB license.
